To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the RT in a visual search experiment is a function of (a) how quickly a subject can determine whether a cluster could contain the item and (b) how quickly a distractor can be rejected once it is determined that it could not contain the item.

a hierarchical cluster tree model for item selection can explain both constant and linear search rate functions, and can explain the variation in search time with distractor ratio in conjunction searches.

(a) a hierarchical clustering model can explain the data from visual search experiments; (b) this model can explain the difference in search rate between conjunction and feature search; and (c) the model can also explain the difference in RT for conjunction search as a function of distractor ratio.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how visual attention is controlled in visual search tasks.
the question of how the brain processes visual information.
the question of how we search for objects in the visual environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a hierarchical clustering model of item selection is an accurate model for visual search, and is a good candidate for a theory of the selection process in visual search.
a two-stage selection-identification model provides a simple and effective account for the results of visual search.
the present study provides a simple and general framework for understanding the search process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the model can explain the results in visual search experiments, and the results can be used to test the model.
the model provides a good fit to the data for a variety of different search tasks, and is able to account both for constant and linear RT set size functions.

a clustering model provides a simple and unified framework for visual search, which accounts for a wide range of experimental results, including constant and linear RTs, conjunction searches, and the effect of distractor ratios.
The main takeaway from our work is that
search rate is not a simple function of the number distractor items, but rather depends on a more complex process of selecting items that might contain the target.
the clustering process is an important part of search and should be incorporated into models of search.
search is best thought of as a hierarchical process, in which items first need to be selected and then recognized.
